accuracy.reason: Primary documentation supports embedded execution, flexible/STRICT typing, explicit foreign-key enforcement, qualified durability, single-writer limits and live-backup hazards. Four supplied diagrams correctly distinguish process boundaries, writer serialization, WAL/checkpoint flow and a candidate composite index; captions avoid universal performance or concurrency guarantees.

evidence.quote: Before starting a transaction, enable enforcement on each connection with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, then query PRAGMA foreign_keys and check that it returns 1.
Committed changes survive failures according to the configured guarantees.

mechanisms.reason: Actors and state changes are sufficient to trace local SQL, constraint enforcement, commit/rollback, writer contention, WAL/checkpoint and backup failure. Long-reader checkpoint delay is stated correctly but its snapshot-protection cause is only implicit, limiting depth rather than leaving a required objective untaught.

evidence.quote: Records original data so SQLite can undo an interrupted change.
Transfers logged changes into the main database file. Long-running reads can delay checkpoint progress and allow the log to grow.
Committed data may still be in the WAL, so copying only the main file can omit required state.

coherence.reason: All nine objectives form a connected progression: process/locality, declared data rules, transaction guarantees, writer coordination, journal mechanics, access costs, operations and selection. Whole-stack evidence resolves early fit questions using later limits; no recurring scenario is necessary. Diagrams reinforce these same relationships.

evidence.quote: SQLite changes where the database runs. You still have a relational database.
But each database allows only one active writer at a time.
Explain where the data lives, who writes it, and how failures are handled.

decisions.reason: Trade-offs include deployment simplicity, one-writer contention, bounded failure handling, storage-dependent durability, index costs, synchronization and tested recovery. Learner transfers these to conditional single-host and multi-server choices without unsupported capacity thresholds.

evidence.quote: Waiting does not create another writer or guarantee success.
Indexes take space and add write maintenance; avoiding a network call does not make expensive work free.
Often a better fit when many machines need shared database access or competing writes cannot take turns.

clarity.reason: Concise definitions and limitations suit the stated SQL-aware audience. Affinity, STRICT, transaction guarantees, WAL, checkpoint and query plan are explained; diagrams supply useful process and index examples without unnecessary story repetition.

evidence.quote: Here, this means there is no separate database server to manage.
Match columns and their order to actual filters and requested ordering; a composite index contains multiple columns.

outcomes.reason: C1-C2: learner explains in-process calls, persistent local files, optional memory and SQL/transactions. C3: query-plan and final answers explicitly retain permissions, capacity and recovery. C4-C5: local applications and a local application server are contrasted with shared multi-server access. C6: workload/writer competition replaces user/size cutoffs and independent copies require synchronization. Covers embedded-database and local-fit objectives using slides 1-2, 5-6, 8-9.

C1: ordinary affinity/storage classes and STRICT conversions/ANY distinguished. C2-C4: primary key, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, missing-value handling and per-connection foreign-key enable/verify explained; declared rules do not replace transaction logic. C5-C6: atomic group, commit/rollback, declared consistency and qualified isolation explained. C7-C8: flush/locking/configuration dependence and external-side-effect boundary stated. Covers typing-and-constraints and acid-and-boundaries objectives from slides 3-4 and journaling context in 6.

C1-C2: multiple connections/readers, one writer, competition and busy access failure explained. C3-C4: short writes, no slow network work, bounded waits, transaction retry and no success guarantee; final answer supplies sustained-demand rejection. C5-C6: original-data undo contrasted with separate-log changes and snapshot reader/writer overlap; diagram connects writer to WAL to main file. C7-C8: checkpoint transfer, old-reader delay/growth and same-host shared-memory/reliable-locking assumptions stated. A complete filesystem checklist is outside the criterion. Covers single-writer and journal-and-wal objectives, slides 4-6 and 9.

C1-C2: defines index/plan, proposes owner/time composite order, inspects EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN and measures representative queries. C3-C4: scan suitability and index CPU/I/O/memory/write/space costs addressed. C5-C6: permissions/capacity/recovery and coordinated version-aware schema changes retained. C7: explains committed WAL state absent from main file and selects a supported consistent backup; criterion permits this alternative without a quiescence procedure. C8: retention, restoration/application usability and recovery-time proof addressed. Covers local-query-plans and safe-operation objectives, slides 1, 7-8 and index diagram.

C1: conditional single-host/occasional-write fit with local access and no separate service. C2: sustained multi-server writes favor client/server; WAL adds neither writers nor network synchronization. C3: constraints, verified foreign keys, transactions, measured indexes and tested consistent recovery included. C4: identifies deployment/data sharing, contention/duration and busy waits, representative query/resource measurement and recovery targets to verify; no numeric threshold invented. Whole-stack query measurement supplies performance evaluation. Covers integrated choose-by-access objective, slides 2-9.

sourceChecks.claim: Live whentouse and linked about.html confirm in-process SQL library, ordinary persistent files and local storage. Diagram correctly places SQLite inside the application versus a separate database server.
Live appropriate-use guidance supports device/desktop storage and application-local website use; deployment locality and competing writes determine suitability.

Live STRICT page confirms affinity conversion, unconvertible ordinary-table values and STRICT/ANY behavior. Linked foreignkeys.html verifies per-connection enable/query outside transactions; linked CREATE TABLE verifies CHECK permits NULL and NOT NULL rejects it.

Live synchronous documentation confirms reduced synchronization can lose committed data after power failure. Linked transactional and isolation documentation support grouped atomicity and visibility; whentouse documents unreliable-locking corruption. Guarantees are explicitly qualified by storage/configuration.

Live isolation documentation confirms multiple connections/processes, single writer, BUSY_SNAPSHOT and transaction restart. Linked busy_timeout reference confirms timeout can end in SQLITE_BUSY. Writer diagram shows serialized access without promising eventual success.

Live WAL sections 2.1-2.2 confirm original-data rollback, log appends, stable snapshots, one writer, checkpoint transfer, long-reader delays and same-host coordination. Diagram correctly shows writer to WAL to checkpoint to main file, with readers using database plus WAL.

Live queryplanner confirms composite search/sort paths; linked optoverview and EXPLAIN document cost-based scan choice and plan inspection. Customer/date diagram is a valid candidate for equality filtering and date ordering, explicitly subject to evaluation.

Live backup documentation supports consistent online snapshots. WAL section 4 confirms separated main/WAL files can lose committed data or corrupt; linked ALTER TABLE describes rebuild/copy migrations and compatibility. Restore testing is appropriate operational guidance, not a claimed engine guarantee.

Live selection checklist favors client/server for direct access across machines or writes that cannot take turns, while allowing SQLite behind a local application server. No arbitrary user limit or automatic replication promise is made.
